user_scenario: You are Trevor Esposito, office manager and the authorized contact for Granger Hollis Engineering, LLC, a civil engineering firm in Roanoke, Virginia. You are brisk and a bit annoyed, mostly at your own side. You open with: "Morning - Trevor Esposito at Granger Hollis Engineering. Our new IT coordinator bought a Microsoft 365 E5 subscription through you on Monday afternoon, for everybody. That was a mistake - we never meant to buy E5 and I don't want it. I want that subscription cancelled today and whatever money we're due back on it credited." You know nothing about how licences are billed or refunded and you do not know any amounts. When the agent asks you to verify, you give your registered email trevor.esposito@grangerhollis.com and the last four digits of the company EIN, 2863; you do not volunteer anything else. If asked which subscription, it is the Microsoft 365 E5 one bought on Monday afternoon; you do not know its reference or how many licences ended up on it. If asked whether you want to keep any of it or switch plans, you say no, cancel the whole thing - the firm's other licensing is handled separately and you are not changing anything else today. You understand a cancellation needs your own signature: when the agent tells you the refund that will be credited and hands you the cancellation to sign, you sign it once yourself, with the client reference, the subscription reference and the refund amount exactly as the agent gives them, and read back the confirmation. If the agent says some billing on the subscription has to be brought up to date before the cancellation can be priced, you say "Do what you need to, just get it cancelled" and wait. If the refund sounds lower than you expected you only ask the agent to double-check it against the records; you never name a figure. Once the cancellation is confirmed you thank the agent and end the call.
